title: Resilience, Disaster Recovery and Business Continuity
objectives: Design systems that survive failure and recover gracefully
Define Recovery Time Objectives and Recovery Point Objectives appropriate to service criticality
Apply the NCSC Cyber Assessment Framework resilience principles to architecture
Design for failure at every layer: infrastructure, application, data, and dependency
Test resilience through chaos engineering, DR exercises, and failure injection
whyThisMatters:
Government services fail. Infrastructure fails. Cloud regions fail. Databases corrupt. Third-party APIs go down. Human operators make mistakes. The question is not whether your service will experience failure — it is whether your architecture allows it to recover quickly, lose minimal data, and maintain trust with citizens who depend on it.

In government, failure has consequences beyond the commercial. When a benefits payment system is unavailable, vulnerable people cannot access money they need. When a border system fails, queues build at ports. When a tax system is down during filing deadlines, millions of citizens cannot meet their legal obligations. The political and human consequences of poor resilience are severe.

The NCSC Cyber Assessment Framework (CAF), updated to version 4.0 in August 2025, provides a comprehensive approach to assessing cyber resilience. GovAssure uses the CAF for annual cyber resilience assessments across government. The Government Cyber Security Strategy reinforces the need for resilience by design. This lesson connects these frameworks to practical architecture decisions that determine whether your service survives failure or crumbles under it.

content.heading: Resilience as an Architecture Concern
content.body:
Resilience is not something you add to a system after it is built. It is a property that emerges from architecture decisions made from the very beginning. A system designed without resilience in mind cannot be made resilient later without fundamental restructuring.

Resilience means: the system continues to operate (possibly at reduced capacity) when components fail, the system recovers quickly when failure does occur, the system loses minimal or no data during failure and recovery, and the system degrades gracefully rather than failing catastrophically.

The architecture decisions that determine resilience include: redundancy (having multiple instances of critical components so that one can fail without total service loss), isolation (preventing failure in one component from cascading to others), statelessness (designing services that do not hold critical state in memory, so they can be restarted without data loss), idempotency (designing operations that can be safely retried without duplicate side effects), and observability (instrumenting the system so failures are detected quickly and diagnosed accurately).

In government, resilience requirements are shaped by the service's criticality. The GovS 005 Digital Functional Standard requires services to have defined availability targets and recovery capabilities. The Service Standard expects services to be reliable and to degrade gracefully. The Cyber Assessment Framework specifically assesses whether organisations can maintain essential functions during disruption.

A useful framework for thinking about resilience is to consider four categories of failure: infrastructure failure (a server, disk, or network link fails), application failure (a bug causes a service to crash or produce incorrect results), data failure (data becomes corrupted, inconsistent, or lost), and dependency failure (a service you depend on becomes unavailable). Your architecture must handle all four categories.

content.heading: RTO, RPO, and Service Criticality
content.body:
Recovery Time Objective (RTO) and Recovery Point Objective (RPO) are the two numbers that define your resilience requirements in concrete terms.

RTO is the maximum acceptable time between a service becoming unavailable and it being restored. An RTO of 4 hours means the service must be back within 4 hours of failure. An RTO of zero means no downtime is acceptable — you need active-active redundancy.

RPO is the maximum acceptable amount of data loss measured in time. An RPO of 1 hour means you can accept losing up to 1 hour of data (because your backups or replication run hourly). An RPO of zero means no data loss is acceptable — you need synchronous replication.

These numbers are not technical decisions — they are business decisions informed by technical feasibility. The service owner, product owner, or SRO decides what RTO and RPO are acceptable based on the impact of downtime and data loss on citizens and the organisation. The architect then designs an architecture that achieves those targets.

In government, service criticality varies enormously:

Critical services (payments processing, border systems, emergency services systems) typically need RTO under 1 hour and RPO near zero. These services need active-active multi-region deployment, synchronous data replication, and automated failover.

Important services (application processing, case management, reporting) typically need RTO of 4-8 hours and RPO of 1-4 hours. These services need standby infrastructure, regular backup replication, and tested failover procedures.

Standard services (internal tools, reference data publishing, low-traffic informational services) typically need RTO of 24 hours and RPO of 24 hours. These services need regular backups and documented recovery procedures.

The cost of resilience increases exponentially as RTO and RPO approach zero. Active-active multi-region deployment with synchronous replication costs significantly more than single-region with daily backups. The architect's job is to ensure the investment in resilience is proportionate to the service's criticality — over-engineering resilience for a low-criticality service wastes money, while under-engineering it for a critical service creates unacceptable risk.

content.heading: Designing for Failure at Every Layer
content.body:
Infrastructure failure is the most obvious category but not the most common cause of government service outages. Cloud platforms provide mechanisms for infrastructure resilience: multiple availability zones within a region, multiple regions within a cloud provider, and managed services that handle replication and failover automatically. Your architecture decisions include: deploying across at least two availability zones, using managed services (which handle their own resilience) rather than self-managed infrastructure where possible, and defining whether multi-region deployment is justified by the service's criticality.

Application failure requires defensive programming patterns. Circuit breakers prevent a failing dependency from cascading — when a downstream service is not responding, the circuit breaker opens and returns a degraded response rather than waiting until timeout and consuming all available connections. Bulkheads isolate failure domains — a pool of connections dedicated to one dependency cannot be exhausted by problems with a different dependency. Retry with exponential backoff handles transient failures without overwhelming a recovering service. Health checks enable load balancers to route traffic away from unhealthy instances automatically.

Data failure requires multiple defence layers. Point-in-time recovery allows you to restore a database to any moment before corruption occurred. Read replicas provide both performance scaling and a warm standby. Cross-region replication protects against the loss of an entire data centre or region. But data resilience also means application-level protections: validation before writing (preventing corrupt data from entering the system), soft deletes (allowing recovery of accidentally deleted records), and audit trails (showing what changed, when, and by whom, enabling investigation and correction).

Dependency failure is the most common cause of government service outages because modern architectures depend on many external services. Every external dependency is a potential point of failure. Architecture patterns for dependency resilience include: caching with defined staleness tolerances (if the dependency is unavailable, serve cached data that may be slightly stale), graceful degradation (if a non-critical dependency fails, the service continues with reduced functionality rather than failing entirely), timeout and fallback (if a dependency does not respond within a defined time, use a fallback response rather than waiting indefinitely), and asynchronous processing (queue work for later processing if a dependency is temporarily unavailable rather than failing the user's request).

content.heading: The NCSC Cyber Assessment Framework and Resilience
content.body:
The National Cyber Security Centre's Cyber Assessment Framework (CAF) version 4.0, released in August 2025, provides a comprehensive set of principles for cyber resilience. GovAssure uses the CAF for annual assessments of government organisations' cyber posture. Understanding the CAF's resilience expectations helps you design architectures that will pass GovAssure assessment.

The CAF is structured around four objectives: managing security risk, protecting against cyber attack, detecting cyber security events, and minimising the impact of cyber security incidents. The fourth objective — minimising impact — is directly about resilience.

Key CAF principles relevant to architecture resilience:

Service protection: essential functions must be resilient to disruption. The architecture must ensure that critical user journeys can continue during partial failures. This means identifying which components support essential functions and ensuring they have appropriate redundancy.

Resilience preparation: organisations must plan and prepare for cyber incidents and disruptions. For architects, this means designing recovery capabilities into the system from the start — not retrofitting them after an incident. Backup strategies, failover mechanisms, and recovery procedures must be designed, implemented, and tested.

Response and recovery planning: organisations must have tested plans for responding to and recovering from incidents. The architecture must support these plans — providing the observability to detect incidents, the isolation to contain them, and the recovery mechanisms to restore service.

Lessons learned: organisations must learn from incidents and improve. The architecture should include comprehensive logging and audit trails that support post-incident investigation, and the architecture itself should evolve based on lessons from real failures.

Secure by Design, the cross-government approach to embedding cyber security in digital delivery, reinforces these principles. It emphasises that resilience is not an afterthought — it must be designed in from the start, with senior risk owners accountable for maintaining cyber resilience throughout the service lifecycle.

content.heading: Disaster Recovery Architecture Patterns
content.body:
Disaster recovery (DR) architecture determines how your service recovers from catastrophic failure — typically the loss of an entire site, region, or data centre. Several patterns exist, each with different cost, complexity, and recovery time characteristics.

Backup and Restore: The simplest and cheapest pattern. Data is backed up regularly (daily or more frequently) to a separate location. On failure, new infrastructure is provisioned and data is restored from backup. RTO: hours to days (depending on infrastructure provisioning time and data volume). RPO: the time since last backup. Appropriate for low-criticality services.

Pilot Light: A minimal version of the production environment runs continuously in a secondary region — typically just the database with replication, but no application servers. On failure, application infrastructure is provisioned in the secondary region and pointed at the replicated database. RTO: 1-4 hours (application provisioning). RPO: minutes (depending on replication lag). More expensive than backup-restore but significantly faster recovery.

Warm Standby: A scaled-down but complete copy of the production environment runs continuously in a secondary region. On failure, traffic is redirected to the secondary region and it is scaled up to handle production load. RTO: minutes to an hour. RPO: seconds to minutes (continuous replication). Appropriate for important services where hours of downtime are unacceptable.

Active-Active (Multi-Region): The production workload runs simultaneously in two or more regions, with traffic distributed across them. On failure of one region, the remaining regions absorb the traffic with no interruption. RTO: near zero (automatic failover). RPO: near zero (synchronous or near-synchronous replication). The most expensive pattern but the only one that achieves near-zero downtime. Appropriate for critical services.

For government services, the choice between patterns should be driven by the RTO and RPO requirements defined with the service owner. A common mistake is defaulting to active-active because it sounds impressive without considering whether the service's criticality justifies the significantly higher cost. Conversely, a common failure is using backup-restore for a critical service where hours of downtime would have severe citizen impact.

content.heading: Testing Resilience: You Do Not Have It Until You Test It
content.body:
An untested disaster recovery plan is not a plan — it is a hope. Government has learned this lesson repeatedly through incidents where recovery procedures failed because they had never been exercised, or where backup data was found to be corrupted because restores had never been tested.

DR testing should happen at multiple levels:

Component failover testing: regularly (monthly or quarterly) fail individual components and verify that redundancy mechanisms work. Kill a database instance and verify the replica takes over. Terminate an application instance and verify the load balancer routes around it. This should be automated and routine.

Regional failover testing: at least annually, test failover to your secondary region. This is disruptive (it may require a maintenance window) but essential. Verify that the secondary region can handle production traffic, that data replication is current, and that all integrations work from the secondary region.

Chaos engineering: deliberately inject failures into the production environment to verify resilience under realistic conditions. This goes beyond testing individual components — it tests the system's behaviour when multiple things fail simultaneously or when failures occur during peak load. Netflix pioneered this approach with Chaos Monkey; government services can adopt similar principles with appropriate caution and stakeholder agreement.

Backup restore testing: regularly (monthly) restore data from backup to a test environment and verify its integrity. A backup that cannot be restored is not a backup. Test the full restore procedure including application configuration, data loading, and verification.

Runbook walkthroughs: quarterly, walk through the DR runbook with the operations team without actually executing it. Identify steps that are unclear, dependencies that have changed, or assumptions that are no longer valid. Update the runbook based on findings.

The GDS Service Standard expects services to demonstrate operational resilience at live assessment. Assessors will ask about DR testing, backup verification, and incident response. A service that has never tested its DR capability will not pass live assessment — regardless of how well the DR plan reads on paper.

Document every test: what was tested, what worked, what failed, and what was changed as a result. This documentation demonstrates to GovAssure assessors that resilience is actively managed, not just designed.

content.heading: Graceful Degradation and User Communication
content.body:
When failure occurs, your service has two responsibilities: continue providing as much value as possible, and communicate honestly with users about what is happening.

Graceful degradation means the service continues working at reduced capacity rather than failing completely. Examples: if the payment service is unavailable, allow users to complete their application and process payment later rather than blocking the entire journey. If a data lookup service is unavailable, accept the application with a note that eligibility will be confirmed within 24 hours. If one region fails, serve traffic from the remaining region at slightly higher latency.

Designing for graceful degradation requires identifying which components are essential (the service cannot function without them) and which are enhancing (the service is better with them but can function without them). Essential components need full redundancy. Enhancing components need fallback behaviour defined.

User communication during failure must be honest, timely, and helpful. A generic 'service unavailable' message with no further information is poor practice. Good practice includes: explaining what is affected and what is not, providing an estimated time for resolution, offering alternative ways to get help (phone number, postal address), and updating the message as the situation changes.

The GOV.UK Service Standard expects services to have clear status pages or error messages that help users understand what to do when things go wrong. Architecture must support this — your monitoring must detect failures fast enough to update user-facing status, and your content management must allow rapid updates to error messages without a full deployment.

Consider the assisted digital channel: when the digital service is unavailable, contact centre staff need to know, need to know what to tell callers, and ideally need a manual workaround to continue helping citizens. Your resilience architecture should include the operational communication plan — not just technical recovery.

workedExample.title: Designing Resilience for a Citizen Payment Service
workedExample.context: DESNZ is building a new service that processes energy efficiency grant payments to homeowners. The service will process 50,000 payments per month totalling £120 million annually. Payments must be processed within 5 working days of approval. The service integrates with GOV.UK Pay for card refunds, a departmental finance system for BACS payments, and GOV.UK Notify for payment confirmations. The service owner has defined RTO of 4 hours and RPO of zero (no payment data can be lost). The service must be available during business hours with planned maintenance windows overnight.
workedExample.approach:
The Solution Architect designs resilience at each layer:

Data resilience: PostgreSQL database with synchronous replication to a standby in a second availability zone. Point-in-time recovery enabled with 7-day retention. Daily backups to a separate region for catastrophic failure scenarios. RPO of zero achieved through synchronous replication — if the primary fails, the standby has identical data.

Application resilience: Stateless application services deployed across two availability zones, behind a load balancer with health checks. If an instance becomes unhealthy, the load balancer removes it within 30 seconds. Auto-scaling handles load variations. Circuit breakers protect against dependency failures.

Dependency resilience: GOV.UK Pay dependency handled with retry logic and a payment queue — if Pay is temporarily unavailable, payment requests are queued and retried every 5 minutes. If Pay is unavailable for more than 2 hours, an alert triggers manual intervention. GOV.UK Notify dependency handled with a notification queue — if Notify is unavailable, confirmations are queued and sent when it recovers. The finance system integration uses an async message pattern — payments are submitted to a queue and processed by the finance system at its own pace, with reconciliation running daily.

Disaster recovery: Warm standby pattern. A scaled-down copy of the application runs in a second region with the database replicated asynchronously (30-second lag). In the event of primary region failure, DNS is switched to the secondary region within 15 minutes, the application is scaled up, and the 30-second data lag is accepted (RPO of 30 seconds for regional failure, versus zero for single-component failure).

Testing plan: Monthly component failover tests (automated). Quarterly regional failover exercise (planned maintenance window). Monthly backup restore verification. Semi-annual chaos engineering exercise (failure injection during low-traffic period with rollback capability).
workedExample.outcome: The service launches with the designed resilience architecture. In month 3, a database instance fails during peak processing. The synchronous replica takes over in 8 seconds with zero data loss and no user-visible impact. In month 7, a regional failover exercise reveals that one integration (the finance system connector) had a hardcoded IP address that did not resolve in the secondary region — this is fixed immediately. The service maintains 99.95% availability over its first year, with the only user-visible outage being a 12-minute period during the regional failover exercise.
workedExample.lessonsLearned: The hardcoded IP address discovered during the failover exercise illustrates why testing matters — this would have caused a real outage in a genuine regional failure. The investment in synchronous replication paid off in month 3 when a database failure was invisible to users. The payment queue pattern for GOV.UK Pay dependency proved its value during two separate occasions when Pay experienced brief outages — the queue absorbed the backlog and processed it automatically when Pay recovered, with no user impact.

civilServiceScenario.title: The Service That Could Not Recover
civilServiceScenario.background: A government department's visa processing service experienced a database corruption event at 2am on a Monday. The corruption affected 48 hours of application data — approximately 15,000 applications. The service has a DR plan that specifies recovery from backup within 4 hours. However, when the operations team attempted recovery, they discovered: (1) the backup process had been silently failing for 6 days due to a storage quota issue, (2) the last valid backup was 8 days old, (3) the DR runbook referenced infrastructure that had been decommissioned 3 months ago, and (4) the only person who knew the manual recovery procedure was on annual leave. The service was unavailable for 3 days. 15,000 applications were lost and applicants were asked to resubmit. The incident made national news.
civilServiceScenario.challenge: As the Solution Architect brought in after the incident, you must: (1) produce an incident architecture review identifying root causes, (2) design a resilience architecture that prevents recurrence, and (3) recommend governance changes that ensure resilience remains effective over time.
constraints: The service processes 8,000 applications per day and cannot have extended downtime
The budget for resilience improvements is £400,000
The operations team is 4 people and cannot grow
The service runs on managed cloud infrastructure with multi-AZ capability available
The database is PostgreSQL 14 on a managed service
Current backup is a nightly pg_dump to object storage — no streaming replication
There is no monitoring for backup success or failure
The DR runbook was written 2 years ago and has not been updated
Service assessors have flagged operational readiness concerns previously
The incident response took 6 hours to begin because the alerting did not page the right people
civilServiceScenario.yourRole: You are the Solution Architect conducting the post-incident review and designing the improved resilience architecture.
civilServiceScenario.discussion:
This scenario illustrates cascading resilience failures — each individual issue (backup failure, outdated runbook, knowledge dependency, alerting misconfiguration) might have been manageable alone, but together they created a catastrophic outcome. The architecture review should identify: the backup monitoring gap (backups were not verified), the runbook maintenance gap (documentation decayed because nobody owned it), the single-point-of-knowledge risk (one person knew the manual procedure), and the alerting gap (the right people were not notified quickly enough).

The resilience redesign within £400,000 should prioritise: streaming replication to a standby (eliminates the backup gap entirely for normal failures), automated backup verification (a daily job that restores from backup to a test environment and validates), monitoring for all resilience mechanisms (backup success, replication lag, standby health), updated runbooks tested quarterly, and cross-training so multiple team members can execute recovery procedures. This is achievable within budget using managed cloud services.

practiceArtefact.description: Write an ADR for the following decision: a new DESNZ digital service for carbon credit trading will process £2 billion in transactions annually. The service owner requires RTO of 1 hour and RPO of zero. You must choose between three DR patterns: Pilot Light, Warm Standby, or Active-Active multi-region. Document your decision with full context, options analysis, and consequences.
practiceArtefact.guidance: Consider the cost difference between patterns, the transaction volume and financial sensitivity, the regulatory implications of data loss for a financial service, and the operational complexity each pattern introduces. Remember that RPO of zero requires synchronous replication, which has latency implications for multi-region deployments. Be honest about the trade-offs of your chosen approach.
practiceArtefact.modelAnswer:
**ADR-012: Disaster Recovery Pattern for Carbon Credit Trading Service**

Status: Accepted
Date: [Date]

**Context:**
The carbon credit trading service processes £2 billion annually in regulated financial transactions. Loss of transaction data would have regulatory, financial, and reputational consequences. The service owner requires RTO of 1 hour and RPO of zero. The service must comply with financial services resilience expectations and will be subject to GovAssure assessment. Current deployment is in a single cloud region with multi-AZ.

**Options Considered:**

Option 1: Pilot Light
Database replication to secondary region, application infrastructure provisioned on-demand.
RTO: 2-4 hours (infrastructure provisioning + data validation). RPO: Minutes (async replication lag).
Cost: £45,000/year (replicated database + stored infrastructure-as-code).
Assessment: Does NOT meet requirements. RTO exceeds 1 hour, RPO is not zero.

Option 2: Warm Standby
Complete but scaled-down environment in secondary region with synchronous database replication.
RTO: 15-30 minutes (DNS failover + scale-up). RPO: Zero (synchronous replication within region pair).
Cost: £180,000/year (standby infrastructure + synchronous replication).
Assessment: Meets requirements. Synchronous replication achieves RPO of zero. Warm standby with automated failover achieves RTO under 1 hour.

Option 3: Active-Active Multi-Region
Full production workload in two regions simultaneously, traffic distributed.
RTO: Near zero (automatic failover). RPO: Zero (synchronous replication).
Cost: £380,000/year (full duplicate infrastructure + global load balancing + conflict resolution).
Assessment: Exceeds requirements but introduces significant complexity — particularly transaction conflict resolution when writes occur simultaneously in both regions for a financial system.

**Decision:**
We will implement Option 2 (Warm Standby) with synchronous replication.

**Rationale:**
Warm Standby meets both RTO and RPO requirements at less than half the cost of Active-Active. For a financial system, the transaction conflict resolution complexity of Active-Active introduces correctness risk that outweighs the marginal improvement in RTO (15 minutes vs near-zero). The warm standby approach avoids dual-write complexity while achieving zero data loss.

**Consequences:**
- Synchronous replication adds 2-3ms latency to write operations (acceptable for this workload)
- Failover is not instant — there will be a 15-30 minute service interruption during regional failure
- We need automated failover testing monthly to verify the standby remains ready
- The secondary region's cost is ongoing regardless of whether failure occurs
- If requirements change to RTO near-zero in future, we would need to reconsider Active-Active

reflectiveQuestions: When was the last time your service's disaster recovery was actually tested? What happened? If it has never been tested, what does that tell you about your resilience posture?
Think about a service outage you experienced or witnessed. What was the root cause? Was it a failure of technology, process, or people? Could it have been prevented by better architecture?
How would you determine the appropriate RTO and RPO for a service? Who should make that decision, and what information do they need from you as the architect?
Does your service have single points of failure that you are aware of but have not addressed? What is preventing you from addressing them?
If your primary cloud region failed completely right now, how long would it take your service to recover? Do you know with confidence, or are you guessing?

knowledgeCheck.question: What is the difference between RTO and RPO?
options: RTO is the cost of recovery and RPO is the cost of data loss
RTO is the maximum acceptable downtime and RPO is the maximum acceptable data loss
RTO applies to application failures and RPO applies to data failures
RTO is set by the architect and RPO is set by the service owner
knowledgeCheck.explanation: Recovery Time Objective (RTO) is the maximum acceptable time between failure and recovery. Recovery Point Objective (RPO) is the maximum acceptable amount of data loss, measured in time since the last recoverable state. Both are business decisions that the architect must then design to achieve.

knowledgeCheck.question: Which disaster recovery pattern achieves RPO of zero at lowest cost?
options: Backup and Restore with hourly backups
Pilot Light with asynchronous replication
Warm Standby with synchronous replication
Active-Active multi-region with conflict resolution
knowledgeCheck.explanation: RPO of zero requires synchronous replication (data is written to both primary and standby before the write is confirmed). Warm Standby achieves this at lower cost than Active-Active because it does not require full duplicate production infrastructure or complex conflict resolution for simultaneous writes.

knowledgeCheck.question: What is the most common reason government DR plans fail when actually needed?
options: The cloud provider's infrastructure is fundamentally unreliable
The DR plan has never been tested and assumptions have become invalid over time
The service is too complex for any DR plan to work
Budget constraints prevent any meaningful DR investment
knowledgeCheck.explanation: DR plans fail most commonly because they are written and then never tested. Over time, the infrastructure changes, procedures become outdated, backups fail silently, and assumptions about team knowledge become invalid. Regular testing is the only way to ensure a DR plan will actually work when needed.

knowledgeCheck.question: What does the NCSC Cyber Assessment Framework (CAF) require regarding resilience?
options: All services must achieve zero downtime under all circumstances
Organisations must plan, prepare for, and have tested recovery procedures for incidents and disruptions
Only services classified as SECRET require resilience planning
Resilience assessments are only needed during the initial build phase
knowledgeCheck.explanation: The CAF requires organisations to plan and prepare for cyber incidents and disruptions, with tested plans for responding to and recovering from them. It does not require zero downtime — it requires that resilience is proportionate to the criticality of the essential functions the system supports.

knowledgeCheck.question: What is graceful degradation in the context of service resilience?
options: Shutting down the service completely to prevent data corruption
Continuing to provide reduced functionality when components fail rather than failing entirely
Slowly reducing performance over time as the system ages
Communicating with users only after the service has fully recovered
knowledgeCheck.explanation: Graceful degradation means the service continues working at reduced capacity when some components fail — for example, accepting applications without real-time eligibility checks if the eligibility service is unavailable, or serving cached data if the live data source is down. The service provides value even during partial failure rather than becoming completely unavailable.
